column1: Per-genome Wright's Nc and GC3 (243 MAGs); expected Nc from GC3 alone by Wright's curve
Nc_exp = 2 + s + 29/(s^2 + (1-s)^2), s = GC3/100. Residual = Nc_observed - Nc_expected.
A more negative residual means MORE codon bias than base composition alone predicts, i.e. stronger selected bias.
Two results, both negative for a simple reduced-Ne reading of the raw Nc gap:
(1) The residual is slightly MORE negative in FSM than RGM, the opposite of the direction predicted if
selection on codon usage were less efficient in FSM. The higher raw Nc in FSM tracks its lower GC3.
(2) After phylogenetic correction none of the three differs between clades (lambda ~ 1; FSM is one origin).
The Wright curve is also a weak null at the extreme GC3 of this genus (81-86%), which limits how much
weight the residual itself can carry. The conclusion is that genome-wide codon statistics do not provide
independent support for reduced Ne in FSM; the branch-based RELAX contrast, which models the tree, does.

Note on bases: the per-genome block above ships 95 FSM and 97 RGM MAGs, the genomes carrying the 20 ribosomal-protein genes the bulk-minus-ribosomal gap requires; its medians are 38.39 (FSM) and 36.56 (RGM), the values plotted in Fig. 4b and quoted in the text as a 1.8-codon difference. The S12b and S12c summary rows are computed on a 96/97/50-genome panel that also covers SGM and give 38.3 and 36.4; the two bases differ by about 0.1 codons and must not be mixed. The three Decay rows are the host-restricted clade (Mycobacterium leprae, M. lepromatosis, M. uberis), computed by the same procedure from the same Bakta 1.11.4 / database 6.0 annotation; their bulk Nc reproduces the 51.3-51.6 recorded in Table S10.
